name: Chapter 1: Electric Charges and Fields
description: Charge and its properties, Coulomb’s law, superposition, electric field and field lines, flux, dipoles, Gauss’s law and its applications

cards.term: Why do you get a shock touching a car door after sliding off the seat?
cards.definition: Discharge through your body of charge built up by rubbing of insulating surfaces (static electricity)

cards.term: What does electrostatics study?
cards.definition: Forces, fields and potentials arising from static charges

cards.term: Who first noticed that rubbed amber attracts light objects? Origin of the word “electricity”?
cards.definition: Thales of Miletus, about 600 BC; from Greek elektron = amber

cards.term: Glass rod rubbed with silk vs plastic rod rubbed with fur: what do they do to each other?
cards.definition: Attract (unlike charges); two glass rods or two plastic rods repel

cards.text: Like charges {{c1::repel}}; unlike charges {{c2::attract}}. The property that distinguishes the two kinds of charge is called {{c3::polarity}}.

cards.term: Who named charges positive and negative? Why those names?
cards.definition: Benjamin Franklin: the two kinds cancel each other when brought in contact, like + and − numbers

cards.term: Frictional electricity: signs by convention
cards.definition: Glass rod (rubbed with silk): positive; Silk: negative; Plastic rod (rubbed with fur): negative; Cat’s fur: positive

cards.term: Identify this device and how it shows charge.
cards.definition: Gold-leaf electroscope: charge flows down the rod to the leaves, which diverge; divergence indicates the amount of charge

cards.term: Figure 1.2(a) · Gold-leaf electroscope
What actually moves when a glass rod is rubbed with silk?
cards.definition: Electrons move from the rod to the silk: rod becomes +, silk −. No charge is created

cards.term: Which everyday forces are basically electrical?
cards.definition: Forces holding atoms and molecules together, glue adhesion, surface tension, contact forces, friction

cards.term: Does rubbing transfer a large share of a body’s electrons?
cards.definition: No: only a very small fraction of the electrons is transferred

cards.term: Conductors vs insulators?
cards.definition: Conductors: charges (electrons) move freely — metals, human body, earth. Insulators: high resistance — glass, porcelain, plastic, nylon, wood

cards.term: Charge given to a conductor vs an insulator: where does it go?
cards.definition: Conductor: spreads over the whole surface. Insulator: stays where it was put

cards.term: Why does a metal spoon held in the hand not get charged on rubbing?
cards.definition: The charge leaks through your body to earth (both conductors); with an insulating handle it does charge

cards.term: What is the third category besides conductors and insulators?
cards.definition: Semiconductors: resistance intermediate between the two

cards.term: Mobile charges in metals vs electrolytes?
cards.definition: Metals: electrons. Electrolytes: both positive and negative ions

cards.term: When can a charged body be treated as a point charge?
cards.definition: When its size is very small compared with the distances involved

cards.text: Three basic properties of electric charge: {{c1::additivity}}, {{c2::conservation}} and {{c3::quantisation}}.

cards.term: Additivity of charge: how is it like mass, and how is it unlike mass?
cards.definition: Like mass: a scalar that adds algebraically. Unlike mass: charge can be negative, so signs matter

cards.term: Total charge of +1, +2, −3, +4, −5 (same units)?
cards.definition: −1

cards.term: State conservation of charge.
cards.definition: The total charge of an isolated system never changes; charge carriers can be created or destroyed only in equal and opposite pairs

cards.term: A neutron decays into a proton and an electron. Is charge conserved?
State quantisation of charge.
cards.definition: \( q = ne \), n an integer: every free charge is an integral multiple of e

cards.term: Who suggested and who demonstrated quantisation of charge?
cards.definition: Suggested by Faraday’s laws of electrolysis; demonstrated by Millikan (1912, oil-drop experiment)

cards.term: Value of e (NCERT) and number of electrons in 1 C?
cards.definition: e = 1.602192 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; about 6 × 10¹⁸ electrons in −1 C

cards.term: Update: is e still a measured constant in SI?
cards.definition: No: since the 2019 SI redefinition, e is fixed exactly at 1.602176634 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Use 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C in problems

cards.term: Define 1 coulomb (via current).
cards.definition: Charge flowing through a wire in 1 s when the current is 1 A: 1 C = 1 A s

cards.term: Why can quantisation be ignored for macroscopic charges?
cards.definition: 1 μC ≈ 10¹³ e: steps of e are too tiny to notice, so charge looks continuous (like a dotted line from far away)

cards.term: Update: quarks carry ±e/3 and ±2e/3. Does this break q = ne?
cards.definition: Not for free charges: quarks are always confined inside hadrons, so every observed free charge is still a multiple of e

cards.term: Example 1.1: 10⁹ electrons leave a body every second. Time to collect 1 C?
cards.definition: 1 / (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ C/s) = 6.25 × 10⁹ s ≈ 200 years: 1 C is a huge unit

cards.term: Example 1.2: total positive (and negative) charge in a cup of water (250 g)?
cards.definition: (250/18) × 6.02 × 10²³ × 10 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ ≈ 1.34 × 10⁷ C (10 protons, 10 electrons per molecule)

cards.term: Roughly how many electrons in a 1 cm³ copper cube?
cards.definition: About 2.5 × 10²⁴

cards.term: Exercise 1.11: polythene rubbed with wool gets −3 × 10⁻⁷ C. Electrons transferred? Mass transferred?
cards.definition: 1.9 × 10¹² electrons, from wool to polythene. Yes, mass is transferred, but only ~2 × 10⁻¹⁸ kg (negligible)

cards.term: Exercise 1.5: glass rubbed with silk — how is charging consistent with conservation?
cards.definition: Electrons are only transferred: the rod’s + charge exactly equals the silk’s − charge; the total stays zero

cards.term: State Coulomb’s law.
cards.definition: Force between two point charges ∝ product of charges, ∝ 1/r², along the line joining them: \( F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{|q_1 q_2|}{r^2} \)

cards.term: What instrument did Coulomb use? Who else used it?
cards.definition: A torsion balance; later Cavendish used one to measure gravitational force

cards.term: Coulomb did not know the charges. How did he vary them?
cards.definition: By touching a charged sphere with an identical uncharged sphere: charge halves each time (q/2, q/4…) — relying on additivity and conservation

cards.term: Values of k and ε₀?
cards.definition: \( k = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \approx 9\times10^{9} \) N m² C⁻²; ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²

cards.term: What is ε₀ called?
cards.definition: Permittivity of free space

cards.term: Force between two 1 C charges 1 m apart in vacuum?
cards.definition: 9 × 10⁹ N — why 1 C is far too big for electrostatics (use μC, mC)

cards.term: Vector form of Coulomb’s law: force on q₂ due to q₁?
cards.definition: \( \vec F_{21} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r_{21}^2}\,\hat r_{21} \), with \( \hat r_{21} \) pointing from 1 to 2

cards.term: Why does the vector form need no separate formula for attraction?
cards.definition: If q₁q₂ < 0, F₂₁ points along \( -\hat r_{21} \) (towards q₁): the sign of q₁q₂ handles it

cards.term: Does Coulomb’s law obey Newton’s third law?
Down to what distance has Coulomb’s law been verified?
cards.definition: Subatomic distances, r ~ 10⁻¹⁰ m (and below)

cards.term: Charles Augustin de Coulomb: nationality, first career, year of the law?
cards.definition: French physicist, earlier a military engineer (West Indies); inverse-square law in 1785

cards.term: Who anticipated Coulomb’s law?
cards.definition: Priestley and Cavendish (Cavendish never published)

cards.term: Example 1.3: ratio of electric to gravitational force, electron–proton? proton–proton?
cards.definition: \( \dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 G m_e m_p} \approx 2.4\times10^{39} \); for two protons ≈ 1.3 × 10³⁶ — independent of distance

cards.term: Example 1.3(b): accelerations of an electron and a proton 1 Å apart (mutual attraction)?
cards.definition: F = 2.3 × 10⁻⁸ N; aₑ ≈ 2.5 × 10²² m/s², aₚ ≈ 1.4 × 10¹⁹ m/s² — gravity is negligible

cards.term: Force between two protons inside a nucleus (~10⁻¹⁵ m apart)? Why don’t they fly apart?
cards.definition: Fₑ ≈ 230 N (F_G ~ 10⁻³⁴ N); the strong nuclear force (range ~10⁻¹⁴ m) holds them

cards.term: Why does gravity dominate large scales if it is 10³⁹ times weaker?
cards.definition: Gravity is always attractive; electric forces come in both signs and cancel in neutral matter

cards.term: Example 1.4: charges on A and B are both halved by touching identical neutral spheres, and the separation is halved. New force?
cards.definition: Unchanged: (¼)/(¼) = 1

cards.term: Coulomb force scaling (Exercise 1.12)
cards.definition: F = 1.5 × 10⁻² N; with 2q, 2q and r/2 the force becomes 16F = 0.24 N

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Exercise 1.12 · scaling

Find the missing step.

Two spheres each 6.5 × 10⁻⁷ C, 50 cm apart. Force? Then each charge doubled and distance halved?
  1. F = 9 × 10⁹ × (6.5 × 10⁻⁷)² / 0.5²
  2. F = 1.5 × 10⁻² N
  3. ?
  4. New F = 16 × 1.5 × 10⁻² = 0.24 N
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Exercise 1.12 · scaling

Find the missing step.

Two spheres each 6.5 × 10⁻⁷ C, 50 cm apart. Force? Then each charge doubled and distance halved?
  1. F = 9 × 10⁹ × (6.5 × 10⁻⁷)² / 0.5²
  2. F = 1.5 × 10⁻² N
  3. Doubling both charges → ×4; halving r → ×4
  4. New F = 16 × 1.5 × 10⁻² = 0.24 N

cards.term: Exercise 1.1: 2 × 10⁻⁷ C and 3 × 10⁻⁷ C, 30 cm apart in air. Force?
cards.definition: 6 × 10⁻³ N, repulsive

cards.term: Exercise 1.2: 0.4 μC and −0.8 μC attract with 0.2 N. Separation? Force on the second?
cards.definition: r = 12 cm; 0.2 N, attractive (towards the first) — Newton’s third law

cards.term: Exercise 1.3: what does the dimensionless ratio ke²/(G mₑ mₚ) ≈ 2.3 × 10³⁹ signify?
cards.definition: Electric force between an electron and proton is ~10³⁹ times the gravitational force between them, at any distance

cards.term: Points to ponder: why is k so large (why is 1 C so big)?
cards.definition: The coulomb is defined through the ampere (magnetic effects, which are much weaker than electric ones); 1 A is sensible, 1 C = 1 A s is huge electrically

cards.term: Update: NCERT says the ampere is defined via the force between current-carrying wires. Still true?
cards.definition: Not since 2019: the SI now fixes e exactly; the ampere (and coulomb) follow from e. k ≈ 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² is unchanged

cards.term: State the principle of superposition (forces).
cards.definition: Force on a charge = vector sum of the forces from each other charge taken one at a time, each unaffected by the others

cards.term: Points to ponder: superposition says two things beyond “add vectors”. What?
cards.definition: (1) Each pair force is unaffected by other charges; (2) there are no extra three-body (or more) forces

cards.term: “All of electrostatics is basically a consequence of…”?
cards.definition: Coulomb’s law and the superposition principle

cards.term: Example 1.5: equal charges q at the corners of an equilateral triangle. Force on Q at the centroid?
cards.definition: Zero — by symmetry (rotate the figure by 120°: the answer must not change)

cards.term: Example 1.6: q, q, −q at the corners of an equilateral triangle. Net force on each? Sum of all three?
cards.definition: F on each q, √3 F on −q (F = q²/4πε₀l²); the three forces add to zero (Newton’s third law)

cards.term: Exercise 1.6: +2, −5, +2, −5 μC at corners A, B, C, D of a 10 cm square. Force on 1 μC at the centre?
cards.definition: Zero: equal charges at opposite corners cancel in pairs

cards.term: Define electric field at a point.
cards.definition: Force per unit positive test charge: \( \vec E = \lim_{q\to0}\dfrac{\vec F}{q} \)

cards.term: Why take the limit q → 0 for the test charge?
cards.definition: So the test charge does not disturb the source charges; F/q stays finite

cards.term: Field of a point charge Q?
cards.definition: \( \vec E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{Q}{r^2}\hat r \): radially outward for +Q, inward for −Q

cards.term: SI unit of electric field (two forms)?
cards.definition: N C⁻¹ = V m⁻¹

cards.term: Source charge vs test charge?
cards.definition: Source: produces the field. Test: small charge used to detect it

cards.term: Does the field of Q depend on the test charge q?
cards.definition: No: F ∝ q, so F/q is independent of q; E depends only on position

cards.term: What symmetry does the field of a point charge have?
cards.definition: Spherical: |E| is the same everywhere on a sphere centred on the charge

cards.term: Field due to a system of charges?
cards.definition: Vector sum: \( \vec E(\vec r) = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\sum_i \dfrac{q_i}{r_{iP}^2}\hat r_{iP} \)

cards.term: Physical significance: why are fields “real” and not just a device?
cards.definition: Beyond electrostatics, effects travel at speed c: fields account for the time delay, carry energy and have their own dynamics

cards.term: Who introduced the concept of field?
cards.definition: Faraday

cards.term: Example 1.7: electron and proton each fall 1.5 cm in a 2 × 10⁴ N/C field. Times of fall?
cards.definition: tₑ = 2.9 × 10⁻⁹ s, tₚ = 1.3 × 10⁻⁷ s (t = √(2hm/eE))

cards.term: Example 1.7: how does fall in an electric field differ from free fall under gravity?
cards.definition: Time depends on mass (a = eE/m): the heavier proton takes longer. In free fall, time is independent of mass

cards.term: Why can gravity be ignored in Example 1.7?
cards.definition: aₚ = eE/mₚ ≈ 1.9 × 10¹² m/s² ≫ g

cards.term: Field midway between +q and −q (Example 1.8)
cards.definition: Both fields point towards −q and add: 7.2 × 10⁴ N/C

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 1.8 · two charges

Find the missing step.

+10⁻⁸ C and −10⁻⁸ C, 0.1 m apart. Field at A, midway between them?
  1. Each charge is 0.05 m from A
  2. E from each = 9 × 10⁹ × 10⁻⁸ / 0.05² = 3.6 × 10⁴ N/C
  3. ?
  4. EA = 7.2 × 10⁴ N/C, towards the negative charge
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 1.8 · two charges

Find the missing step.

+10⁻⁸ C and −10⁻⁸ C, 0.1 m apart. Field at A, midway between them?
  1. Each charge is 0.05 m from A
  2. E from each = 9 × 10⁹ × 10⁻⁸ / 0.05² = 3.6 × 10⁴ N/C
  3. Both point from + towards −, so they add
  4. EA = 7.2 × 10⁴ N/C, towards the negative charge

cards.term: Example 1.8: fields at B (5 cm outside the + charge) and C (0.1 m from both)?
cards.definition: E_B = 3.6 × 10⁴ − 0.4 × 10⁴ = 3.2 × 10⁴ N/C away from the pair; E_C = 9 × 10³ N/C parallel to the line (+ to −)

cards.term: Exercise 1.8: +3 μC and −3 μC, 20 cm apart. Field at the midpoint? Force on −1.5 × 10⁻⁹ C there?
cards.definition: E = 5.4 × 10⁶ N/C towards the negative charge; F = 8.1 × 10⁻³ N towards the positive charge

cards.term: Define an electric field line.
cards.definition: A curve whose tangent at each point gives the direction of the net field there (arrow gives the sense)

cards.term: How do field lines show field strength?
cards.definition: By their density (lines per unit area normal to them): crowded = strong, spread out = weak

cards.term: Why is the number of field lines crossing any sphere around a point charge the same?
cards.definition: E ∝ 1/r² while the area ∝ r²: lines per area fall as 1/r² — the field lines picture builds in the inverse-square law

cards.term: Define solid angle.
cards.definition: \( \Delta\Omega = \Delta S/r^2 \) (area on a sphere ÷ radius²); unit steradian

cards.term: What did Faraday call field lines? Why is the modern name better?
cards.definition: “Lines of force” — misleading, especially for magnetic fields; “field lines” is preferred

cards.text: Field lines start on {{c1::positive}} charges and end on {{c2::negative}} charges (or at infinity for a single charge).

cards.term: Why can two field lines never cross?
cards.definition: The field at the crossing would have two directions — impossible, E is unique

cards.term: Why can’t electrostatic field lines form closed loops?
cards.definition: The electrostatic field is conservative (Chapter 2)

cards.term: Exercise 1.7(a): why can’t a field line have sudden breaks?
cards.definition: A break would mean E suddenly vanishes; in a charge-free region E varies continuously, so lines are continuous

cards.term: What do field lines look like in a uniform field?
cards.definition: Equally spaced parallel straight lines

cards.term: Identify: field lines of which configuration?
cards.definition: Positive point charge (q > 0): radially outward

cards.term: Identify: field lines of which configuration?
cards.definition: Negative point charge (q < 0): radially inward

cards.term: Identify: field lines of which configuration? What does it show?
cards.definition: Two equal positive charges: lines bend away, a neutral point midway — pictures repulsion

cards.term: Identify: field lines of which configuration? What does it show?
cards.definition: Electric dipole (+q, −q): lines go from + to −, picturing attraction

cards.term: Is a field line the path a charge follows?
cards.definition: Not in general: it gives the direction of force (acceleration), not velocity. Only a charge released from rest in straight field lines follows the line

cards.term: Exercise 1.13 (Fig 1.30): signs of the three particles? Largest q/m?
cards.definition: 1 and 2 bend towards the + plate → negative; 3 bends towards − → positive. Particle 3 deflects most → largest q/m

cards.term: Define electric flux through a small area.
cards.definition: \( \Delta\phi = \vec E\cdot\Delta\vec S = E\,\Delta S\cos\theta \), θ between E and the normal

cards.term: What does flux measure pictorially?
cards.definition: The number of field lines crossing the area (proportional to, not equal to)

cards.term: Direction of an area vector? For a closed surface?
cards.definition: Along the normal; for a closed surface, the outward normal

cards.term: When is the flux through a flat area zero?
cards.definition: When E is parallel to the surface (θ = 90° with the normal)

cards.term: Unit and dimensions of electric flux?
cards.definition: N C⁻¹ m² = V m; [ML³T⁻³A⁻¹]

cards.term: Liquid flux analogy: what is different about electric flux?
cards.definition: Nothing physical actually flows in electric flux

cards.term: Exercise 1.14: E = 3 × 10³ î N/C through a 10 cm square. Flux if the plane is parallel to yz? If the normal is at 60° to x?
cards.definition: 30 N m²/C; 15 N m²/C (× cos 60°)

cards.term: Exercise 1.15: flux of the same uniform field through a 20 cm cube?
cards.definition: Zero: what enters one face leaves the opposite one

cards.term: Define an electric dipole and its dipole moment.
cards.definition: Charges +q and −q separated by 2a; \( \vec p = q\times 2a\,\hat p \), directed from −q to +q

cards.term: Unit and dimensions of dipole moment?
cards.definition: C m; [LTA]

cards.term: Total charge of a dipole is zero. Is its field zero?
cards.definition: No: the charges are separated, so their fields don’t cancel exactly; far away it falls as 1/r³

cards.term: Dipole field on the axis (exact and r ≫ a)?
cards.definition: \( E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{4qar}{(r^2-a^2)^2} \to \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{2p}{r^3} \), along p

cards.term: Dipole field on the equatorial plane (exact and r ≫ a)?
cards.definition: \( E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{p}{(r^2+a^2)^{3/2}} \to \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{p}{r^3} \), opposite to p

cards.term: Mnemonic: axial vs equatorial dipole field at the same large r?
cards.definition: “Axis is double, equator is reversed”: E_axial = 2 E_equatorial, and the equatorial field points opposite to p

cards.term: Why does the dipole field fall as 1/r³ instead of 1/r²?
cards.definition: Far away the +q and −q fields nearly cancel; only their small difference (∝ separation/r) survives, adding one more power of r

cards.term: What is a point dipole?
cards.definition: 2a → 0 and q → ∞ with p = 2qa finite; the r ≫ a formulas become exact for all r

cards.term: Polar vs non-polar molecules?
cards.definition: Polar: permanent dipole moment, e.g. H₂O. Non-polar: centres of + and − coincide, e.g. CO₂, CH₄ (get induced dipoles in a field)

cards.term: Example 1.9: ±10 μC, 5 mm apart. Field 15 cm away on the axis and on the equatorial line?
cards.definition: Axis: 2.6 × 10⁵ N/C along p. Equator: 1.33 × 10⁵ N/C opposite to p (exact and r ≫ a answers agree since r/a = 60)

cards.term: Exercise 1.9: +2.5 × 10⁻⁷ C at (0, 0, −15 cm), −2.5 × 10⁻⁷ C at (0, 0, +15 cm). Total charge and dipole moment?
cards.definition: Total 0; p = 2.5 × 10⁻⁷ × 0.30 = 7.5 × 10⁻⁸ C m along −z (− to +)

cards.term: Dipole in a uniform field: net force and torque?
cards.definition: Net force zero; torque \( \vec\tau = \vec p\times\vec E \), |τ| = pE sin θ

cards.term: What does the torque on a dipole try to do? When is it zero?
cards.definition: Align p along E; zero when p ∥ E or antiparallel

cards.term: Dipole in a non-uniform field with p ∥ E or antiparallel: net force?
cards.definition: p ∥ E: force towards increasing field. p antiparallel: towards decreasing field. Torque zero in both

cards.term: Why does a charged comb attract uncharged bits of paper?
cards.definition: The comb polarises the paper (induced dipole along E), and its field is non-uniform, so the dipole is pulled towards the stronger field — the comb

cards.term: Exercise 1.10: p = 4 × 10⁻⁹ C m at 30° to E = 5 × 10⁴ N/C. Torque?
cards.definition: τ = pE sin 30° = 10⁻⁴ N m

cards.term: Linear, surface and volume charge densities
cards.definition: Linear λ: ΔQ/Δl, C m⁻¹; Surface σ: ΔQ/ΔS, C m⁻²; Volume ρ: ΔQ/ΔV, C m⁻³

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Fig. 1.21 · charge densities

Definition and unit?

Linear λ?
Surface σ?
Volume ρ?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Fig. 1.21 · charge densities

Definition and unit?

Linear λΔQ/Δl, C m⁻¹
Surface σΔQ/ΔS, C m⁻²
Volume ρΔQ/ΔV, C m⁻³

cards.term: Identify the three kinds of charge distribution shown.
cards.definition: Line (ΔQ = λΔl), surface (ΔQ = σΔS), volume (ΔQ = ρΔV)

cards.term: How small is the element ΔS used to define σ?
cards.definition: Small macroscopically but large enough to contain very many microscopic charges: σ is a smoothed average that ignores quantisation

cards.term: Field of a continuous distribution?
cards.definition: \( \vec E \approx \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\sum \dfrac{\rho\,\Delta V}{r'^2}\hat r' \) — Coulomb + superposition, an integral in the limit

cards.term: Points to ponder: where is the electric field undefined or discontinuous?
cards.definition: Undefined at the location of a point charge discontinuous across a surface charge defined everywhere inside a volume distribution

cards.term: Flux through a sphere of radius r around a point charge q at its centre?
cards.definition: \( \phi = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2}\cdot 4\pi r^2 = \dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0} \) — independent of r

cards.term: State Gauss’s law.
cards.definition: Flux through any closed surface = \( \dfrac{q_{enc}}{\varepsilon_0} \), where q_enc is the total charge enclosed

cards.term: Uniform field through a closed cylinder with axis along E: net flux?
cards.definition: −ES (entry face) + ES (exit face) + 0 (curved) = 0: no enclosed charge

cards.term: Gauss’s law: whose field appears in the flux, and whose charge on the right side?
cards.definition: E is due to all charges, inside and outside; q counts only the charge inside

cards.term: What is a Gaussian surface? One restriction on choosing it?
cards.definition: Any closed surface used to apply Gauss’s law; it must not pass through a discrete point charge (field undefined there), though it may cut a continuous distribution

cards.term: When is Gauss’s law useful for finding E?
cards.definition: When the charge distribution has symmetry (spherical, cylindrical, planar)

cards.term: On what property of Coulomb’s law does Gauss’s law rest?
cards.definition: The inverse-square dependence; a violation of Gauss’s law would signal a departure from 1/r²

cards.term: Exercise 1.16(b): zero net flux out of a box. Is there no charge inside?
cards.definition: Not necessarily: the net charge is zero; equal + and − charges could be inside

cards.term: Charge q at the centre of a cube. Flux through one face?
cards.definition: \( \dfrac{q}{6\varepsilon_0} \) by symmetry (Exercise 1.17: +10 μC 5 cm above a 10 cm square → 1.9 × 10⁵ N m²/C)

cards.term: Flux of a non-uniform field through a cube (Example 1.10)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 1.10 · non-uniform field

Find the missing step.

Eₓ = αx^½ (α = 800 N C⁻¹ m^-½), Eᵧ = E_z = 0. Cube of side a = 0.1 m from x = a to x = 2a. Charge inside?
  1. Only the two faces normal to x have flux
  2. ?
  3. φ = 800 × (0.1)^2.5 × 0.414 = 1.05 N m²/C
  4. q = ε₀φ = 9.27 × 10⁻¹² C
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 1.10 · non-uniform field

Find the missing step.

Eₓ = αx^½ (α = 800 N C⁻¹ m^-½), Eᵧ = E_z = 0. Cube of side a = 0.1 m from x = a to x = 2a. Charge inside?
  1. Only the two faces normal to x have flux
  2. φ = a²(ER − EL) = αa^(5/2)(√2 − 1)
  3. φ = 800 × (0.1)^2.5 × 0.414 = 1.05 N m²/C
  4. q = ε₀φ = 9.27 × 10⁻¹² C

cards.term: Identify: in Example 1.10, which faces of the cube carry flux, and why?
cards.definition: Only the two shaded faces normal to x: E has only an x-component

cards.term: Example 1.11: E = +200 î N/C for x > 0 and −200 î for x < 0; cylinder r = 5 cm, faces at x = ±10 cm. Net flux and charge?
cards.definition: Each face +1.57 N m²/C, side 0 → φ = 3.14 N m²/C; q = ε₀φ = 2.78 × 10⁻¹¹ C

cards.term: Exercise 1.16(a): net outward flux 8.0 × 10³ N m²/C. Charge inside?
cards.definition: q = ε₀φ ≈ 7.1 × 10⁻⁸ C (0.07 μC)

cards.term: Exercise 1.18: 2.0 μC at the centre of a 9.0 cm cube. Net flux?
cards.definition: q/ε₀ ≈ 2.3 × 10⁵ N m²/C — cube size is irrelevant

cards.term: Exercise 1.19: −1.0 × 10³ N m²/C through a 10 cm sphere. With radius doubled? Charge?
cards.definition: Still −1.0 × 10³ N m²/C; q = ε₀φ ≈ −8.8 nC

cards.term: Field of an infinitely long line charge λ? Gaussian surface?
cards.definition: \( E = \dfrac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r} \), radial; a coaxial cylinder (flux only through the curved part)

cards.term: Why must the field of an infinite line charge be radial?
cards.definition: Pairs of elements on either side of P cancel each other’s components along the wire; only radial parts survive

cards.term: Why must the wire be “infinitely long” for E = λ/2πε₀r?
cards.definition: Otherwise end effects spoil symmetry and E is not normal to the curved surface; the result holds near the middle of a long wire

cards.term: Field of an infinite plane sheet σ? Gaussian surface?
cards.definition: \( E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} \), normal to the sheet; a box or cylinder piercing the sheet (flux 2EA)

cards.term: Intuition: why doesn’t the field of an infinite sheet weaken with distance?
cards.definition: Moving away, each patch is farther, but you see more of the sheet at useful angles; the two effects cancel exactly — like a wall of light that never looks dimmer

cards.term: Field of a uniformly charged thin spherical shell, outside?
cards.definition: \( E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r^2} \) (r ≥ R): as if all charge were at the centre

cards.term: Field inside a uniformly charged thin spherical shell?
cards.definition: Zero everywhere inside (Gaussian sphere encloses no charge)

cards.term: Sketch E versus r for a charged spherical shell.
cards.definition: 0 inside, jumps to \( q/4\pi\varepsilon_0R^2 \) at r = R, then falls as 1/r²

cards.term: What does the experimental fact “E = 0 inside a charged shell” confirm?
cards.definition: The 1/r² law of Coulomb (precision tests of the inverse-square law use this)

cards.term: Does the “charge acts from the centre” result hold for a solid uniformly charged sphere?
cards.definition: Yes, for points outside it

cards.term: Fields from Gauss’s law
cards.definition: Infinite line charge λ: λ / 2πε₀r (∝ 1/r); Infinite plane sheet σ: σ / 2ε₀ (constant); Thin shell, outside: q / 4πε₀r² (∝ 1/r²); Thin shell, inside: 0; Two oppositely charged plates, between: σ / ε₀; Two oppositely charged plates, outside: 0

cards.term: Exercise 1.23: two large parallel plates with ±σ on their inner faces (σ = 17.0 × 10⁻²² C/m²). E outside and between?
cards.definition: Outside: 0 (fields of the two sheets cancel); between: σ/ε₀ = 1.9 × 10⁻¹⁰ N/C

cards.term: Example 1.12: atom = point nucleus +Ze with −Ze spread uniformly to radius R. E inside and outside?
cards.definition: \( E = \dfrac{Ze}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\dfrac{1}{r^2} - \dfrac{r}{R^3}\right) \) for r < R (outward); 0 for r > R (neutral)

cards.term: Exercise 1.20: conducting sphere, radius 10 cm; E at 20 cm = 1.5 × 10³ N/C radially inward. Charge?
cards.definition: q = Er²/k = −6.7 nC (inward → negative)

cards.term: Exercise 1.21: sphere of diameter 2.4 m, σ = 80.0 μC/m². Charge and flux leaving?
cards.definition: Q = σ·4πR² ≈ 1.45 × 10⁻³ C; φ = Q/ε₀ ≈ 1.6 × 10⁸ N m²/C

cards.term: Exercise 1.22: line charge gives 9 × 10⁴ N/C at 2 cm. λ?
cards.definition: λ = 2πε₀rE = 10⁻⁷ C/m (0.1 μC/m)

cards.term: Charge is a scalar. What extra invariance does it have that kinetic energy lacks?
cards.definition: Charge is the same in all frames in relative motion; kinetic energy is not

cards.term: Is every scalar conserved? Is every conserved quantity a scalar?
cards.definition: No to both: KE is a scalar but not conserved in inelastic collisions; angular momentum is a conserved vector

cards.term: Is there a quantisation law for mass like that for charge?
cards.definition: No: charge quantisation is a basic (unexplained) law with no mass analogue

cards.term: Why can’t electrons sit on top of protons inside the nucleus?
cards.definition: The laws of quantum mechanics forbid it; this gives atoms their structure

cards.term: Correction: NCERT prints “1 mC (micro coulomb) = 10⁻⁶ C” in Section 1.4.3. Right symbol?
cards.definition: 1 μC = 10⁻⁶ C (micro); 1 mC = 10⁻³ C (milli) — the μ was lost in typesetting

cards.term: Chapter 1 formula sheet
cards.definition: Coulomb’s law: F = kq₁q₂/r², k = 9 × 10⁹; Field of a point charge: E = kq/r²; Dipole moment: p = q × 2a (− to +); Dipole field, axis / equator: 2kp/r³ / kp/r³; Torque on a dipole: τ = p × E; Flux: φ = E·ΔS; Gauss’s law: φ = q_enc/ε₀
